items.answer: (a) Its members have no continuity of interaction, shared identity or organisation. (b) The family is a primary group.
items.markingKey: 4 marks: (a) 2 for the reason – its members have no continuity of interaction, shared identity or organisation. (b) 2 for the corrected statement – The family is a primary group. Credit a relevant supporting fact from the NCERT chapter.

items.stem: What is meant by 'social control' in the context of social control?
items.answer: The various means used by a society to bring its unruly members back into line.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: social control correctly explained as the various means used by a society to bring its unruly members back into line.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
items.answer: II only
items.markingKey: (b) I is incorrect: Gender is an ascribed status. II is correct.

items.stem:
Read the following extract on social control and answer the questions that follow.
"Formal social control is exercised by agencies such as the state, the police and the courts. What counts as deviance varies across societies and over time. Conflict theorists see social control as a means of enforcing the control of dominant groups over the rest of society."
(i) The view that social control is necessary to maintain order in society is associated with the: (1)
(ii) Explain the term 'deviance' as it relates to this theme. (1)
(iii) Explain the reason behind the following: Informal social control is strong in small communities. (2)
items.answer: (i) functionalist perspective (ii) Modes of action that do not conform to the norms or values held by most members of a group or society. (iii) People know each other and are sensitive to gossip, ridicule and praise.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) functionalist perspective (ii) Modes of action that do not conform to the norms or values held by most members of a group or society. (iii) People know each other and are sensitive to gossip, ridicule and praise.

items.stem:
Read the following statements about social stratification:
I. Stratification persists over generations and is supported by patterns of belief.
II. Class membership is fixed at birth and cannot change.
III. Social stratification refers to structured inequalities between groups, not to differences between individuals.
Which of these statements are correct?
items.answer: I and III only
items.markingKey: (d) I is correct. II is incorrect: Class is an open system in which people can move up or down. III is correct.

items.stem: Distinguish between 'status' and 'role'.
items.answer: Status: a socially defined position in a group or society with rights and duties attached to it. Role: the dynamic or behavioural aspect of status; what a person is expected to do in a given status.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: 1 for explaining 'status' (a socially defined position in a group or society with rights and duties attached to it.) and 1 for 'role' (the dynamic or behavioural aspect of status; what a person is expected to do in a given status.), with the contrast made clear.

items.stem:

II. The family is an example of a secondary group.
III. Community refers to close personal relationships, while society refers to impersonal and contractual relationships.
Which of these statements are correct?
items.answer: I and III only
items.markingKey: (d) I is correct. II is incorrect: The family is a primary group. III is correct.

Read the following extract on social groups, community and society and answer the questions that follow.
"A quasi-group such as a social class can become a social group when its members become organised. Relationships in a primary group are personal and intimate, while those in a secondary group are impersonal. An aggregate is a collection of people who happen to be in the same place at the same time but have no definite links."
(i) The group whose way of life a person aspires to without belonging to it is called a: (1)
(ii) Explain the term 'out-group' as it relates to this theme. (1)

items.answer: (i) reference group (ii) A group to which a person does not belong, described as 'they'. (iii) They aspire to the lifestyle and status of that group.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) reference group (ii) A group to which a person does not belong, described as 'they'. (iii) They aspire to the lifestyle and status of that group.

items.stem: Which term describes the following? The movement of individuals or groups from one social position to another.
items.answer: social mobility
items.markingKey: (c) social mobility: the movement of individuals or groups from one social position to another.

items.stem:
Study the extract below and answer the questions.
"Role stereotyping limits people to roles seen as suitable for their group. In traditional societies ascribed status tends to matter more, while modern societies give more scope to achieved status. Role conflict arises when the expectations of two or more roles clash. Ascribed status is assigned at birth or involuntarily, while achieved status is gained through effort."
(i) Explain the term 'role stereotyping', which is related to the theme of the extract. (1)
(ii) Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain the following: Role stereotyping restricts individuals. (1)
(iii) A student concludes: "Prestige attached to an occupation is the same in all societies." Use your knowledge of the chapter to evaluate this conclusion. (2)
items.answer: (i) Fixing the role of a group, such as women as homemakers and men as breadwinners. (ii) It fixes roles for whole groups, such as women as homemakers, regardless of individual abilities. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: It varies across societies and changes over time.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) Fixing the role of a group, such as women as homemakers and men as breadwinners. (ii) It fixes roles for whole groups, such as women as homemakers, regardless of individual abilities. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: It varies across societies and changes over time.

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about status and role is correct?
items.answer: Ascribed status is assigned at birth or involuntarily, while achieved status is gained through effort.
items.markingKey: (b) The others are wrong: Gender is an ascribed status. It arises when the expectations of different roles clash. Ascribed status matters more in traditional societies; modern societies give more scope to achieved status.
options: Gender is an example of achieved status.
Ascribed status is assigned at birth or involuntarily, while achieved status is gained through effort.
Role conflict means that a person has only one role.
Achieved status matters more in traditional societies than in modern ones.
